title: Livingston v. Jefferson (1811)
summary: The court applied the historical rule confining the land-trespass action to the place where the land was located.
notes:
The assigned materials discuss later changes to federal venue law. This historical decision is not a substitute for the applicable statutory venue provisions.

Livingston sued former President Jefferson in federal court in Virginia for $100,000, alleging that Jefferson as President had ordered marshals to eject him from land he held in the Territory of Orleans; Marshall (sitting with District Judge Tyler) applied the English local-action rule, so the suit could be brought only in Orleans Territory.

sections.Parties: Livingston sought damages from Jefferson for conduct affecting land outside the forum.
sections.Material Facts: The action was brought in Virginia while the relevant land was in Louisiana. The claim involved alleged trespass concerning that property. The legal barrier turned on the classification of the action as local, rather than solely on the defendant’s amenability to ordinary process.
sections.Procedural History: Chief Justice Marshall, sitting as a circuit justice, applied the traditional rule and declined jurisdiction over the action. The assigned discussion expresses the tension between that result and practical access to a forum.
sections.Issue: Could the land-related action be heard outside the state where the property lay under the inherited local-action doctrine?
sections.Holding: No, under the historical doctrine applied in that decision.
sections.Reasoning: The rule tied a local action to the geographic location of the land. Its formal operation could bar a personal damages claim even when the defendant was available elsewhere. The chapter uses the case to show the historical basis of the later controversy, including judicial reconsideration and statutory changes.

learning.why: The court applied the historical rule confining the land-trespass action to the place where the land was located.

topics.cp-local-actions: The historical local-action rule barred the forum from hearing the foreign-land trespass claim. The result provides the tradition challenged in Reasor-Hill and later altered by statute.
topics.cp-venue: The local-action doctrine is a venue rule confining land actions to the district where the land lies.
